blogs.title: Carbon as a first-class signal: Bringing software carbon intensity to OpenTelemetry
blogs.content: Posted on October 15, 2026 by Diana Todea - CNCF Ambassador, Kepler maintainer, OpenTelemetry Documentation approver and Romanian Localization maintainer At Observability Summit Europe 2026 in Prague, I presented a keynote titled Carbon as a First-Class Signal: Designing a Standard for OpenTelemetry . The talk explored how Software Carbon Intensity (SCI) could become part of cloud-native observability through OpenTelemetry semantic conventions, and how the Green Software Foundation ‘s ongoing work aims to establish a common language for carbon-related telemetry. Cloud-native systems are designed to be observable. We collect metrics, logs, and traces to understand how applications behave, identify performance bottlenecks, and make better decisions about infrastructure. We monitor CPU utilization, memory consumption, request latency, and resource allocation. Yet one important dimension of system efficiency is still largely missing from our operational view: carbon emissions. As sustainability becomes part of the conversation around cloud-native infrastructure, the challenge is no longer simply whether we can measure energy consumption or estimate carbon emissions. It is whether we can connect that information to the workloads, services, and engineering decisions that influence it. This is where Software Carbon Intensity (SCI) and OpenTelemetry could help establish a common approach. Figure 1 – Me speaking at Observability Summit EU The missing signal in observability The cloud-native ecosystem already has tools for collecting energy and infrastructure information. Projects such as Kepler help expose energy-related metrics from Kubernetes environments. Other tools provide information about infrastructure utilization, energy consumption, and the carbon intensity of electricity. However, collecting these measurements is only part of the challenge. Consider a Kubernetes workload that consumes less energy after an optimization. Is the application actually more carbon-efficient? What if the workload processes twice as many requests? What if the electricity powering the infrastructure has a different carbon intensity? And how do we attribute shared infrastructure consumption to individual applications? Traditional observability helps us understand what a system is doing. Energy and carbon measurements introduce additional context, but without a consistent way to associate that information with software activity, comparisons become difficult. We need to move beyond collecting isolated measurements toward understanding the carbon impact of the work our systems perform. Understanding Software Carbon Intensity The Software Carbon Intensity specification from the Green Software Foundation provides a methodology for measuring the carbon emissions associated with software. Rather than considering total emissions alone, SCI relates emissions to a functional unit of software activity. The formula is: Where: E (Energy): Energy consumed by the software. I (Carbon intensity): Carbon emissions associated with the electricity consumed per unit of energy. M (Embodied emissions): Emissions associated with the hardware used by the software, allocated to the activity being measured. R (Functional unit): The unit of work performed, such as a request, transaction, or user. The functional unit is particularly important because it allows us to evaluate carbon efficiency in relation to useful work. Imagine two versions of an application. Version A produces 100 kg CO₂e while processing one million transactions. Version B produces 110 kg CO₂e while processing two million transactions. Although Version B produces more emissions overall, its emissions per transaction are lower: Version A Version B Total emissions 100 kg CO₂e 110 kg CO₂e Transactions 1 million 2 million SCI per transaction 0.0001 kg CO₂e 0.000055 kg CO₂e Version B has a lower carbon intensity per transaction, despite its higher total emissions. Figure 2: Software Carbon Intensity (SCI) This distinction matters when evaluating software optimizations. Reducing total energy consumption and improving efficiency per unit of work are related, but they are not interchangeable objectives. SCI gives engineers a structured way to examine both. Why OpenTelemetry matters OpenTelemetry has helped the cloud-native community establish a common language for collecting and exchanging telemetry. Through its semantic conventions , OpenTelemetry defines how attributes and measurements can be represented consistently across different systems, programming languages, and infrastructure environments. This same approach could help address a significant challenge in software sustainability: making carbon-related information understandable and interoperable. Today, different tools may expose energy consumption, electricity carbon intensity, or estimated emissions using different names, units, and levels of granularity. Even when the underlying measurements are available, connecting them to a particular Kubernetes workload, service, or operation is not straightforward. The SCI for OpenTelemetry initiative explores how SCI concepts could be represented using OpenTelemetry semantic conventions. The goal is not to introduce carbon as a replacement for existing observability signals. Instead, it is to establish a consistent way to describe carbon-related information alongside the operational context engineers already collect. For example, a shared vocabulary could help describe energy consumption, carbon intensity, embodied emissions, and the functional unit used for an SCI calculation. This would make it easier for different implementations to exchange and interpret sustainability information without relying on tool-specific definitions. Importantly, this work is still evolving. The proposed conventions should not be confused with finalized or officially adopted OpenTelemetry semantic conventions. The difficult part: attribution and context One of the most important questions in bringing SCI to OpenTelemetry is how carbon-related information should be attributed to software. In cloud-native environments, infrastructure resources are frequently shared. Multiple workloads can run on the same node, applications can scale dynamically, and services may depend on infrastructure distributed across different locations. Measuring the energy consumption of a physical machine does not automatically tell us how much energy a particular application consumes. Similarly, knowing the carbon intensity of electricity in a region does not directly establish the emissions attributable to an individual service. The SCI for OpenTelemetry community has been examining these questions through a series of discussions focused on scope, use cases, and the information needed to support consistent calculations. Several important themes have emerged. Attribution rather than measurement alone. The challenge is not necessarily to invent new ways to measure energy. It is to establish how existing measurements and estimates can be associated with the software responsible for a particular activity. Support for modeled and estimated values. Not every environment provides direct energy measurements. Some values must be estimated or derived from models. A useful specification needs to account for these differences rather than assume every measurement is directly observed. Provenance and transparency. Engineers need to understand where carbon-related values originate, how they were calculated, and what assumptions were involved. Without this information, comparisons can be misleading. Clear boundaries and units of work. SCI calculations depend on what is included in the measurement and which functional unit is selected. These choices need to be explicit for results to be meaningful. These are not simply naming problems. They influence how carbon information can be interpreted, compared, and used in practice.
